But I wonder how long you would have waited if I had left you alone. When would you have spoken if I had not asked you? My decision to thank you for helping Lydia certainly made a great difference. Too much of a difference, I fear. What happens to the lesson we ought to learn if our happiness comes from my breaking a promise? I should never have mentioned the matter. This will never do.”

“You need not worry. There will be nothing wrong with the lesson. Lady Catherine’s unreasonable attempts to separate us removed all my doubts. I do not owe my present happiness to your eagerness to express your gratitude. I was in no mood to wait for you to give me an opening. What my aunt told me had raised my hopes, and I was determined to learn the truth at once.”

“Lady Catherine has been enormously helpful. That should please her, since she loves to be useful. But tell me, why did you come to Netherfield? Was it simply to ride to Longbourn and feel awkward? Or did you hope for something more serious?”

“My real purpose was to see you and discover, if possible, whether I could ever hope to win your love. The reason I gave, or at least the one I admitted to myself, was to find out whether your sister still cared for Bingley. If she did, I meant to make the confession to him that I have since made.”

“Will you ever find the courage to tell Lady Catherine what awaits her?”

“I am more likely to lack time than courage, Elizabeth. Still, it must be done. Give me a sheet of paper, and I will do it immediately.”

“If I did not have a letter of my own to write, I could sit beside you and admire your beautifully even handwriting, as another young lady once did. But I also have an aunt, and I must not neglect her any longer.”

Elizabeth had still not answered Mrs. Gardiner’s long letter. She had been unwilling to admit how greatly her aunt had overestimated her closeness to Mr. Darcy. Now, however, she had news to share that she knew would be warmly welcomed. She felt almost ashamed to realise that her uncle and aunt had already missed three days of happiness, and immediately wrote:

“My dear aunt, I should have thanked you sooner for your long, kind, and wonderfully clear account of everything. The truth is that I was too annoyed to write. You imagined more than was really there. But now you may imagine as much as you please. Let your fancy roam, and follow every happy possibility that this subject suggests. Unless you suppose I am already married, you cannot be very far wrong.

Emma Woodhouse was beautiful, intelligent, and wealthy, with a pleasant home and a cheerful nature. She seemed to possess many of life’s greatest blessings, and in nearly twenty-one years she had experienced very little trouble or unhappiness.

She was the younger of two daughters of a loving father who indulged her every wish. Since her sister’s marriage, Emma had been in charge of his household, though she was still very young. Her mother had died so long ago that she had only a faint memory of her loving touch. An excellent governess had taken her mother’s place and given her almost a mother’s affection.

Miss Taylor had spent sixteen years with the Woodhouse family, more as a friend than a governess. She loved both girls dearly, but Emma especially. The two were as close as sisters. Even while Miss Taylor was still officially a governess, she had been too gentle to exercise much control. Now that even the appearance of authority had long disappeared, they lived together as deeply devoted friends, and Emma did exactly as she pleased. She thought highly of Miss Taylor’s judgment, but usually followed her own.

The real problems in Emma’s life were, in fact, that she had rather too much freedom to get her own way and a tendency to think a little too highly of herself. These faults threatened to spoil her many pleasures. At present, however, she was so unaware of the danger that she did not consider them misfortunes at all.

Then sorrow came—a gentle sorrow, but one that brought no uncomfortable awareness of her faults. Miss Taylor married. Losing Miss Taylor’s company gave Emma her first experience of grief. On this dear friend’s wedding day, she sat lost in sad thoughts for a sustained time for the first time in her life. When the wedding was over and the bridal party had left, she and her father were alone at dinner, with no third person expected to brighten the long evening. Her father settled down to sleep after the meal, as he usually did, leaving her with nothing to do but think about her loss.

The marriage promised every happiness for her friend. Mr. Weston was a man of excellent character, with a comfortable income, a suitable age, and agreeable manners. Emma could take some satisfaction in remembering how generously she had always wished for and encouraged the match, putting her friend’s happiness before her own. Yet for her, it had been a dreadful morning’s work. She would miss Miss Taylor every hour of every day. She remembered all her kindness and affection over sixteen years: how she had taught her and played with her since she was five, how she had devoted every effort to winning her affection and entertaining her when she was well, and how she had nursed her through the many illnesses of childhood.

After a while you’d wake up and look around to see what had woken you, and maybe spot a steamboat coughing its way upstream, so far over toward the opposite bank that you couldn’t make out anything except whether its wheel was at the back or the side. Then for an hour or so there’d be nothing to hear and nothing to watch—just pure loneliness. Next a raft would come drifting past, way out there, with maybe some fellow chopping on it, because somebody’s nearly always chopping on a raft. You’d see the axe shine and fall, but hear nothing. You’d watch it rise again, and only when it was above the man’s head would the ka-chunk reach you. That was how long the sound took to cross the water. We spent our days that way, lounging around and listening to the quiet. Once a heavy fog came down, and the people on passing rafts and things banged tin pans to keep steamboats from running them over. A flatboat or a raft passed so near that we could hear people talking, swearing, and laughing as clear as anything, without seeing a trace of them. It made your skin creep, like spirits making all that racket in midair. Jim said he thought they were spirits, but I said:

“No, spirits wouldn’t say, ‘Damn this damn fog.’”

As soon as night came we pushed off. Once we’d got the raft near the middle, we left it to drift wherever the current took it. Then we lit our pipes, hung our legs in the water, and talked about all sorts of things. We went naked, day and night, whenever the mosquitoes let us. The new clothes Buck’s family had made me were too fine to feel comfortable, and anyway I never cared much for clothes.

Sometimes we had that whole river to ourselves for ages. Across the water lay the banks and islands, with perhaps a little spark of light—a candle in a cabin window. Now and then you could see a spark or two on the water, on a raft or a flatboat, you know, and perhaps hear somebody fiddling or singing on one of those boats. Living on a raft is wonderful. Above us was the sky, scattered all over with stars. We would lie on our backs looking up and arguing about whether somebody had made them or they’d just happened. Jim reckoned they’d been made, but I figured they’d happened. It seemed to me that making so many would have taken too long.
